title: A Dark-Haired Girl & PKD: Letters from the Heart, the Spleen, and the Funnybone
author: Philip K. Dick; Linda Levy; compiled by Linda Castellani
card_summary: A collection of correspondence between Philip K. Dick and Linda Levy, compiled and edited by Linda Castellani (copyright 2008). The volume is subtitled 'Letters from the Heart, the Spleen, and the Funnybone,' reflecting the emotional and humorous range of the exchange. Organized into sections covering a preface and three labeled sides attributed to PKD, suggesting a structured editorial arrangement of letters across different phases or themes of the correspondence.
page_summary: This fifty-one-page document, compiled and edited by Linda Castellani (copyright 2008), presents the correspondence between Philip K. Dick and Linda Levy under the title 'A Dark-Haired Girl & PKD: Letters from the Heart, the Spleen, and the Funnybone.' Castellani, who is Linda Levy, structured the collection into sections labeled 'PKD, Side One' through 'PKD, Side Four,' plus 'Odds and Ends,' each representing different phases or thematic dimensions of the correspondence. The preface establishes the collection as the first offered for sale by one of Dick's 'dark-haired girls,' with Castellani presenting the original pieces of paper on which the correspondence was written, supplemented by contextual narrative. Each letter is shown with one page partially obscured by puzzle-piece imagery, chosen to reflect what Castellani calls 'the puzzle that was the man himself.' Beyond the letters, the collection includes Castellani's personal copy of The Dark-Haired Girl, two Georg Grosz prints signed by Grosz in pencil, the only known prints of three photographs Dick took of Castellani, and the November 6, 1975 issue of Rolling Stone magazine containing an article on Dick that he sent her a dollar to purchase. The preface references a Paul Giamatti biopic then in development and expresses Castellani's desire to present her account before the film version solidified public perception. She describes Dick as multidimensional, capable of love and longing, meanness and vindictiveness, playfulness and humor, and a brooding darkness that led to outbursts of physical and emotional violence toward women he professed to love. The document quotes from Dick's December 1, 1972 letter to Roger Zelazny, in which Dick describes his search for the dark-haired girl and mentions compiling 127 pages of letters sent to his agent as a sort of journal, originally titled 'The Dark-Haired Girl: A Search for the Authentic Human Being.' The collection provides a unique first-person perspective on Dick's personal relationships during the early 1970s, a period of intense personal upheaval and creative productivity.

## **What the Collection Contains** 

I offer for sale the original pieces of paper on which my personal correspondence from Philip K. Dick was written.  I created this narrative to provide a context for the correspondence, as well as a glimpse at each document. 

For each letter I show one page, with the content partially obscured by a design of puzzle pieces (which seemed appropriate considering the puzzle that was the man himself), plus a thumbnail of each page of the document. 

This collection is being offered in its entirety to preserve the continuity of the events described in the correspondence and the context of those events hinted at in the glimpses of this relationship you are about to see. 

It is also the first collection of its kind offered by one of Dick’s dark-haired girls. 

The collection includes, in addition to the correspondence, my personal copy of The Dark-Haired Girl, two Georg Grosz prints (signed by Grosz in pencil), the only known prints of three photos Phil took of me, and the November 6, 1975 issue of Rolling Stone magazine, with an article on Phil that he sent me a dollar to buy. 

**- 4 -** 

## **Preface** 

I don’t need to tell you that millions of people around the globe have been avidly reading the work of Philip K. Dick for decades, and millions more have been thrilled by the movies that were made from it, notably the iconic films Bladerunner, Total Recall, Minority Report, Screamers, A Scanner Darkly…you know. 

There is a biopic in the works as I write this. How well the script captures Phil, and how faithfully Paul Giamatti portrays him, remains to be seen.  I don’t know what period of time the movie covers, or even if Linda Levy will be a character in the film.
